themes.briefing:
A preventable infant mortality crisis is quietly worsening in the United States, driven by rising vaccine hesitancy and institutional failure to track its consequences. A national study covering more than 5 million births found that the rate of newborns not receiving the vitamin K shot jumped 77 percent between 2017 and 2024, despite the intervention being a standard pediatric recommendation for over six decades[28]. The CDC estimates that unvaccinated newborns are 81 times more likely to develop late vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a condition that causes spontaneous hemorrhaging in the brain[28]. ProPublica's review of autopsy records found that in nearly every case examined, these deaths were preventable — yet state and federal agencies lack coherent tracking systems, leaving the true scale of the problem unmeasured and underreported[28]. The pattern reflects a broader erosion of trust in routine medical interventions, with life-or-death consequences for the most vulnerable population.

A separate but equally systemic failure is playing out in Oklahoma, where a family's newly built home was inundated with thick black oily sludge that seeped through the foundation in August 2025, apparently from an improperly plugged oil well drilled in the 1940s[27]. When the Meredith family sought assistance, the Oklahoma Corporation Commission — the regulatory body nominally responsible for overseeing oil and gas pollution and well plugging — told them it could not help, forcing the family to relocate four times in four months while carrying both mortgage and rental costs simultaneously[27]. The case exposes a staggering regulatory gap: Oklahoma officially lists approximately 19,000 orphan wells under state jurisdiction, but federal researchers estimate the actual number likely exceeds 300,000[27]. The discrepancy between official inventories and ground-truth estimates suggests that contamination events like the one in Fort Gibson are not anomalies but foreseeable consequences of decades of deferred accountability in the oil and gas sector. Together, these cases illustrate a convergent pattern of regulatory institutions failing to protect citizens from well-documented, preventable harms — whether in neonatal care or environmental remediation.

Tiny Footprints, a Blue Blanket: What I Can't Forget About the Babies Who Died of Vitamin K Deficiency

themes.briefing:
The physical costs of AI infrastructure are coming into sharp relief through developments like Utah's Stratos project, a $100 billion data center complex approved by Box Elder County commissioners that would span roughly 40,000 acres near the Great Salt Lake basin.[25] The scale of the undertaking is extraordinary: at full buildout, the facility could demand up to 9 gigawatts of power — exceeding the entire current electricity consumption of Utah — while generating nearly 4,000 formal objections from residents citing water depletion, air quality degradation, and ecological risks to the Great Salt Lake ecosystem.[25] The gap between promoter claims and independent estimates is itself instructive; Kevin O'Leary projected 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent positions, while more measured analyses put those figures at 4,000 and 1,350 respectively.[25] This pattern of inflated economic promises against underweighted environmental liabilities is becoming a signature dynamic in large-scale AI infrastructure siting.

The project's approval pathway also deserves scrutiny. Its advancement through Utah's Military Installation Development Authority, framed under national competitiveness imperatives, raises substantive questions about whether federal security narratives are being used to compress local democratic input on decisions with significant long-term environmental consequences.[25] The Stratos case is an early but indicative example of how the race to build AI compute capacity is generating concentrated physical burdens in specific communities — a distributional problem that existing regulatory frameworks appear poorly equipped to address.

At the consumer layer, the same AI ecosystem that demands this infrastructure is increasingly understood as a driver of behavioral and attentional fragmentation. Stanford educators Bill Burnett and Dave Evans, engaging with the question of how individuals resist the attention economy, frame the problem as one of deliberate habit architecture in the face of platforms engineered for maximum engagement capture.[24] The convergence of these two stories — massive physical infrastructure being built to power systems that then colonize human attention — underscores that AI's costs are neither purely digital nor purely abstract. They are territorial, ecological, and cognitive simultaneously, and policy frameworks that address only one dimension will remain structurally incomplete.

references.title: How to Resist the Attention Economy — with Bill Burnett and Dave Evans

themes.briefing:
The U.S. economy is confronting a compounding set of structural pressures that individually would warrant concern but together suggest a more serious deterioration in the economic foundation. Consumer prices rose 3.8% year-over-year in April — the highest inflation reading in three years — while producer prices climbed 6% over the same period, a spread that signals upstream cost pressures have yet to fully transmit to consumers[22]. Critically, American wages are no longer keeping pace with inflation for the first time in three years, eroding the purchasing power that has sustained consumer spending through prior bouts of price pressure[22]. The political dimension is notable: the current administration's approval on economic management now polls worse than its predecessor's ever did, despite having campaigned explicitly on price reduction — a dynamic that may accelerate policy instability rather than correction[22].

Beneath the inflation headline lies a deeper structural rot in the debt architecture of the American economy. The diagnostic framing gaining traction among analysts is that the United States has shifted from borrowing to invest in the future to borrowing to sustain the present[21]. This manifests at every level simultaneously: the federal government is now making trillion-dollar annual interest payments on accumulated debt, corporations are financing leveraged bets on AI with borrowed capital, and consumers — the most alarming signal — are increasingly financing everyday necessities including groceries and food delivery through credit[21]. This is not a cyclical pattern amenable to rate adjustments; it reflects a structural dependency on debt that compresses future fiscal and monetary flexibility regardless of which party holds power.

The intersection of inflation and debt creates particular vulnerability in equity markets, especially in technology. Big Tech's revenue base remains overwhelmingly tied to advertising — approximately 97% of Meta's revenues and roughly 75% of Google's — meaning any sustained compression of consumer spending directly threatens the valuation architecture of the sector[22]. Broader AI-adjacent investment is simultaneously drawing scrutiny, with credible comparisons being drawn between current AI hardware valuations and the speculative excess of the late 1990s dot-com cycle[22,23]. If inflation persists and consumer spending contracts, the feedback loop through digital advertising could reprice tech assets in ways the market is not yet discounting. The OPEC dimension — specifically the UAE's reported moves away from petrodollar arrangements — adds a further layer of uncertainty to dollar-denominated debt markets, though the full implications remain to be assessed[20].

themes.briefing:
The Supreme Court's electoral footprint is expanding on multiple fronts. Most consequentially, the Court denied Virginia Democrats' request to reinstate the state's new congressional map ahead of the 2026 elections, a decision Governor Abigail Spanberger characterized as effectively nullifying the votes of more than three million Virginians.[19] Separately, the Court sent two Voting Rights Act Section 2 cases back to lower courts for reconsideration in light of its recent 6-3 ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, which substantially narrowed the statute's reach — a remand that drew a pointed dissent from Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who argued the VRA cases turned on the distinct question of Section 2's private enforceability, which Callais did not resolve.[17] Together, these actions signal a Court that is methodically constraining the legal architecture around minority voting rights and electoral map oversight, with downstream consequences that will materialize well before November 2026.

Within the conservative legal coalition, an ideological fracture is sharpening around Justice Neil Gorsuch's promotion of a 'creedal' conception of American national identity — the view that citizenship is grounded in shared ideals rather than ethnicity or heritage.[16] Far-right figures including Curtis Yarvin and Claremont Institute senior fellow Jeremy Carl have attacked this position as a symptom of the 'broad intellectual failure of the conservative legal movement,' framing Gorsuch's rejection of nativism as a betrayal.[16] This tension is not merely academic: with birthright citizenship cases potentially heading to the Court, the hard right's willingness to publicly break with originalist justices like Gorsuch, Barrett, and Roberts reflects a broader stress fracture between the institutional conservative legal establishment and an increasingly illiberal nationalist base that no longer regards judicial restraint as a virtue.[16]

On election integrity, Colorado Governor Jared Polis's decision to commute Tina Peters's sentence draws renewed attention to the mechanics of election denialism at the county level.[15] Peters, who as Mesa County Clerk disabled security cameras and granted unauthorized access to voting machines, built her fraud narrative on grounds that her own county's 2020 results — broadly consistent with 2016 patterns she had accepted as legitimate — plainly did not support.[15] The commutation does not rehabilitate the underlying conduct, but it does illustrate how politically costly accountability for election subversion has become even in states where prosecutions succeeded. The episode is a useful case study in the institutional vulnerabilities that persist when local election officials treat their offices as instruments of political resistance rather than administrative stewardship.[15]

themes.briefing:
Donald Trump's political standing has deteriorated markedly in the opening months of his second term, with quantitative tracking now confirming a sustained erosion of public support. As of May 18, 2026, Trump's net approval rating has reached a second-term low of -20.1, down from -18.6 just two weeks prior, with individual pollsters ranging from -20 (AtlasIntel) to -26 (CBS News/YouGov)[1]. The economic dimension of this decline is particularly acute: his net approval on inflation and cost of living sits at -41.8, while his broader economic approval has hit a new second-term low of -27.4[1]. CBS News/YouGov polling puts his overall approval at 37% against 63% disapproval, with strong disapproval outpacing strong approval by 52% to 20%[5]. Analyst Ron Brownstein has characterized Trump as being 'consistently in a much deeper hole now than other recent presidents who had bad mid-terms,' a judgment reinforced by the trajectory of roughly one percentage point of approval lost per month since January 2026[5].

Beyond the topline numbers, the qualitative texture of public opinion suggests a more durable political liability than cyclical disapproval. Fifty-one percent of Americans now say Trump does not care 'at all' about the needs and problems of people like them, with only 18% saying he cares 'a lot'[5]. Bill Kristol and other center-right analysts argue this reflects a voter recognition that Trump's priorities — personal interests, financial dealings, and score-settling — are systematically misaligned with constituent welfare[3]. Questions about Trump's physical fitness add a further dimension of vulnerability: he turns 80 next month and has made three unexplained dental visits in 2026, received an undisclosed MRI, and has been observed with swollen ankles and apparent episodes of somnolence during televised events[6]. Democratic party committees have thus far declined to amplify these health concerns publicly, choosing to focus messaging on corruption and cost-of-living issues instead[6].

The downstream electoral implications are significant. The Silver Bulletin generic congressional ballot average now stands at D +6.6 — the most Democratic-favorable reading of the current cycle — with individual polls as high as D +11 (New York Times/Siena) and D +14 (AtlasIntel)[2]. The historical analogue is instructive: at the equivalent point in the 2018 cycle, the generic ballot stood at D +6.8, and Democrats ultimately netted 40 House seats[2]. On current trajectory, Democrats are assessed as having a strong probability of retaking the House, though ongoing mid-decade redistricting efforts in several states represent a structural countervailing force[2]. Within the Republican Party, the ideological consolidation around Trump continues unabated — the defeat of Senator Bill Cassidy in the Louisiana GOP primary was immediately cited by Senator Lindsey Graham as proof that the party is unequivocally Trump's[5] — suggesting the institutional GOP lacks both the incentive and the capacity to recalibrate ahead of the midterms, leaving the party's fortunes fully bound to a president whose approval is in freefall.

themes.theme: Trump Foreign Policy: Iran War, China & NATO
themes.briefing:
The Iran conflict has become a significant domestic political liability for the Trump administration, with public opposition reaching nearly 60 percent as of mid-May 2026 — a level of disapproval that, even at the war's outset when opposition stood around 48 percent, was already historically high relative to past American military engagements[8]. The diplomatic situation offers little relief: Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency characterized U.S. negotiating positions as offering 'no tangible concessions,' and Tehran continues to rebuff American terms on uranium enrichment and the Strait of Hormuz blockade, effectively returning the military option to active consideration within the National Security Council[14]. Compounding the strategic picture, energy markets are under acute stress, with U.S. distillate inventories running 11–18 percent below seasonal norms and European gas storage near 30–35 percent of capacity against a normal 55 percent threshold for summer entry — structural vulnerabilities that constrain allied flexibility and elevate the cost of prolonged conflict[14]. Separately, suspicious betting patterns on prediction markets timed to key Iran war developments — including Israel's initial strike, the commencement of U.S. bombing, and a ceasefire announcement — have drawn scrutiny alongside broader questions about the administration's use of material non-public information[10].

On NATO, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's decision to halt the deployment of roughly 4,000 troops to Poland and withdraw an additional 5,000 from Europe has introduced serious strategic incoherence into the alliance relationship. The move was unexpected even within the Pentagon, and it comes at the expense of Poland — a country that has approached the 5 percent of GDP defense spending threshold, subsidizes American forces on its soil, and has spent the past decade building capable eastern-flank capabilities in close coordination with U.S. advisors[9]. Analysts with command-level experience assess that the primary danger is not the force reduction per se but the precedent it sets: using troop deployments as transactional leverage over allied political decisions, particularly European reluctance to endorse U.S. actions in the Middle East. Romania, Bulgaria, the Baltic states, and Croatia have invested heavily in American-designed force structures over the same period, and arbitrary drawdowns risk hollowing out the integrated deterrence architecture those investments were meant to support[9].

On China, the administration's strategic positioning draws sharp criticism from analysts who argue that Trump conflates bilateral trade-balance arithmetic with genuine geopolitical competition. His Beijing visit yielded agreements to export soybeans and energy commodities alongside favorable Nvidia chip-export decisions — an outcome more consistent with mercantile deal-making than a coherent great-power strategy[12]. Critics note that during his first term Trump praised China's COVID-19 response in pursuit of a soybean sale, and the pattern persists: prioritizing commercial optics over structural competition. By contrast, Obama's Trans-Pacific Partnership represented a more coherent framework precisely because it paired sound trade economics with explicit geopolitical skepticism toward Beijing — an approach the current administration has neither revived nor replaced[12]. The Nvidia chip-export decision is additionally complicated by disclosures that Trump purchased between $500,000 and $1 million in Nvidia stock shortly before the Commerce Department authorized those sales to China, a timeline that has intensified ethics scrutiny[10].

big_picture:
The dominant thread running through today's digest is a compounding crisis of institutional credibility — across economic, political, and governance domains — that is now producing measurable, concrete consequences for ordinary Americans. Trump's net approval has sunk to a second-term low of -20.1[1], driven in significant part by economic anxiety that the underlying data validates: consumer prices rose 3.8% year-over-year in April while producer prices climbed 6%, a spread signaling that the worst of upstream cost pressures has not yet reached household budgets[22]. That squeeze is unfolding simultaneously with a quietly worsening public health failure — newborn vitamin K refusal rates up 77% since 2017, leaving infants 81 times more vulnerable to life-threatening bleeding events[28] — suggesting that anti-institutional sentiment has migrated from the political sphere into medical decision-making with potentially fatal results. These are not separate crises; they share a common root in eroded public trust and the downstream costs of that erosion falling hardest on the most vulnerable.

The foreign policy and judicial dimensions of today's digest reinforce this picture of an overstretched and increasingly contested governing order. The Iran conflict, opposed by nearly 60 percent of Americans with diplomatic channels showing little flexibility[8], is consuming political capital the administration cannot afford given its domestic approval trajectory. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court's refusal to reinstate Virginia's new congressional map — effectively freezing a redistricting outcome that Governor Spanberger argued nullified three million votes[19] — illustrates how judicial architecture built over the past decade is now operating as a structural constraint on democratic correction mechanisms. With Voting Rights Act Section 2 cases remanded for reconsideration under a narrowed 6-3 framework[19], the legal landscape for electoral competition heading into the 2026 midterms is being shaped by institutional forces that move independently of public opinion shifts.

The AI infrastructure boom adds a further dimension of structural tension: the scale of projects like Utah's Stratos complex — 40,000 acres, up to 9 gigawatts of demand near an already-stressed Great Salt Lake basin, nearly 4,000 formal objections[25] — suggests that the technological buildout underwriting AI's economic promise is itself generating environmental and democratic friction that has not been priced into policy or public expectations. Taken together, today's briefings describe a political economy under simultaneous pressure from inflation it cannot resolve, a foreign conflict it cannot conclude, judicial constraints it cannot easily overcome, and infrastructure ambitions whose costs are only beginning to materialize. The 2026 midterm environment is forming in this context, and the compounding nature of these pressures means that relief on any single front is unlikely to offset deterioration across the others.
